mainTopic: Debts of the condemned and their heirs, a condemned man's offerings, and the execution of a pregnant woman and her fetus
overview: The amud opens by asking about a ברייתא: does the תנא קמא really think we would bring a man on his way to execution back to court? רב יוסף explains that the argument is whether a מלוה על פה can be collected from יורשין. רבה explains instead that it is about whether a debt written in the תורה counts like one written in a שטר. A ברייתא about a pit-digger whose heirs must pay for an ox is answered: the digger was already judged by a court before he died, even if the judges had to sit at the mouth of the pit. Next, a ברייתא teaches that a condemned man's execution waits only to sprinkle the blood of an offering already slaughtered, because we may not drag out his suffering. A new משנה rules that a pregnant woman's execution is not delayed until she gives birth, unless she is already in labor. The גמרא learns from the word 'גם' that the fetus dies with her, and explains that once labor begins the baby is a separate body. It then discusses שמואל's rule to strike the womb first, and whether a fetus or its mother dies first. The amud ends with שמואל's ruling that on שבת we cut open a woman who died in labor to save the baby, and the גמרא asks why this even needs to be said. The answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Does the first opinion really allow bringing him back to court?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the implication of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's reasoning. If his reason is that the condemned man cannot be returned to court, it sounds like the תנא קמא holds that he can, which is impossible.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean the תנא קמא holds that a man on his way to execution can be brought back to stand before the court?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pointing out a strange implication in the ברייתא. It sounds as if the תנא קמא would stop an execution to hold a new court case about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר said the condemned man is exempt because he can't be brought back to court. That suggests the תנא קמא disagrees and would bring him back. But everyone agrees we do not delay an execution, so the גמרא needs a different explanation of the argument.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication; from the fact that one opinion says X, we infer the other holds the opposite
The first, unnamed opinion in a ברייתא or משנה
Able to be brought back to stand trial before the court

phrases.english: By implication, the first tanna holds:
phrases.notes: This is going back to the ברייתא just before this, about a man being led out to execution who injured someone.

phrases.english: that he can be brought back to stand before the court?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks an inference from רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's reasoning in the preceding ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implied position of the תנא קמא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבי שמעון בן אלעזר exempts because the condemned man can't return to court, the תנא קמא must hold he can. But no one delays an execution.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the argument is about collecting an oral loan from heirs
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף explains that no one delays the execution. The argument is whether the injured person can collect from the יורשין afterward, which depends on whether a מלוה על פה can be collected from heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: They argue about whether a loan made by word of mouth can be collected from the heirs. The תנא קמא holds it can be collected from the heirs. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds it cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question by moving the argument to after the execution. The real question is whether the victim can collect from the condemned man's heirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damages owed without any document are treated like a מלוה על פה, a loan made by word of mouth. The תנא קמא lets that kind of debt be collected from the יורשין, so the victim gets paid. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר does not, so after the execution there is no one to collect from.

keyTerms.meaning: A loan made by word of mouth, with no written document
Collects the debt from the heirs
They disagree about

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Regarding a loan by oral agreement,
whether one collects it from the heirs, they disagree.
The first tanna holds:

phrases.aramaic: מִלְוָה עַל פֶּה גּוֹבֶה מִן הַיּוֹרְשִׁין,
phrases.english: a loan by oral agreement is collected from the heirs,
and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds:
it is not collected from the heirs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: בְּמִלְוָה עַל פֶּה גּוֹבֶה מִן הַיּוֹרְשִׁין קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא by redefining what the מחלוקת is about.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא would bring the condemned man back to court.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees the execution goes ahead. They argue about whether a מלוה על פה can be collected from יורשין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This connects the case to the well-known question of whether an oral debt can be collected from heirs.

steps.title: רבה: the argument is whether a Torah debt counts like a written debt
steps.stepSummary: רבה disagrees with רב יוסף. Everyone agrees an oral loan is not collected from heirs. The argument is whether an obligation written in the תורה, like paying for damages, counts as if it were written in a שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Everyone agrees an oral loan is not collected from the heirs. Here they argue about a debt written in the תורה: is it like one written in a document? The תנא קמא holds it is like a written document. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives a different answer to the same question. He moves the argument to a new issue: how strong is a debt that comes straight from the תורה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A debt written in a שטר can be collected from יורשין, but an oral one cannot, and here everyone agrees on that. The obligation to pay for damages is written in the תורה. The תנא קמא treats that like a שטר, so the heirs pay. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר treats it like an oral loan, so they don't.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
A debt whose obligation is written in the תורה, like damages
A written legal document
Is similar to; is treated like

steps.confusionAlert: רבה is not saying the תנא קמא lets heirs pay oral loans. He says everyone agrees they don't. The תנא קמא simply classifies a תורה obligation as being like a written debt.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
According to everyone, a loan by oral agreement
is not collected from the heirs;
and here, regarding a debt that is written in the Torah,
phrases.notes: He means an obligation the תורה itself creates, like having to pay for damage you caused.

phrases.english: whether it is like one written in a document, they disagree.
The first tanna holds:
it is like one written in a document,
and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds:
it is not like one written in a document.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה אָמַר: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מִלְוָה עַל פֶּה אֵינוֹ גּוֹבֶה מִן הַיּוֹרְשִׁין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the קשיא of step 1 and rejects רב יוסף's framing.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute is about oral loans (רב יוסף).
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees about oral loans. The dispute is whether a מלוה הכתובה בתורה is like a debt written in a שטר.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of a מלוה הכתובה בתורה, a debt created by the תורה itself, comes up in many places in ש״ס.

steps.title: Challenge from the case of a pit dug in a public area
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: if someone digging a pit in רשות הרבים is killed by an ox that falls on him, the ox's owner is פטור, and if the ox dies, the digger's heirs must pay for it. This shows a damages obligation is collected from heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: If someone was digging a pit in a public area and an ox fell on him and killed him, the ox's owner is exempt. Not only that, but if the ox died, the heirs of the pit's owner must pay the ox's value to its owner!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view that a debt from the תורה, like damages, cannot be collected from heirs. It quotes a ברייתא where the heirs clearly must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pit-digger caused damage, and he died before paying. Still, the ברייתא makes his heirs pay for the ox. That suggests a damages obligation from the תורה is collected from heirs, which seems to contradict רבי שמעון בן אלעזר as רבה explained him.

keyTerms.meaning: A pit; one of the main categories of damage
A public area
Exempt from paying
Not only that, but even more

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who digs a pit in the public domain,
and an ox fell on him and killed him, he is exempt,
phrases.notes: The ox fell on the digger, and the one who is exempt is the ox's owner.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא שֶׁאִם מֵת הַשּׁוֹר —
phrases.english: and not only that, but if the ox died,
the heirs of the pit's owner are liable
to pay the value of the ox to its owner!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the position, raised in step 3, that a debt written in the תורה is not collected from heirs.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a מלוה הכתובה בתורה is not collected from יורשין (רבי שמעון בן אלעזר according to רבה)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes the digger's heirs pay for damage caused by his pit. So a damages obligation from the תורה is collected from heirs.

steps.title: The digger already stood trial before he died
steps.stepSummary: רבי אילא in the name of רב answers the challenge to רבה: the ברייתא is a case where the digger was already judged in court, so the debt is like one written in a שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אילא said in the name of רב: the case is where the digger stood trial before he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from the ברייתא in step 4. It says the digger had already been judged by a court before he died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבה's explanation, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that a debt written only in the תורה cannot be collected from heirs. But once a court rules on the debt, it becomes a firm obligation, like a loan with a שטר. That is why the heirs pay in the ברייתא, and that position still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: stood trial, was judged by a court
heirs
a written document of debt

phrases.english: Rabbi Ila said that Rav said:
It is where he stood trial,
phrases.notes: He means the digger was judged for the damage while still alive, so the court's ruling fixed the debt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אִילָא אָמַר רַב כְּשֶׁעָמַד בַּדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא against רבה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the ברייתא to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that a debt written only in the תורה is collected from heirs
steps.terutzMaskana: The heirs pay only because a court had already ruled on the debt, which makes it like a שטר

steps.title: But the ox killed him
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says the ox killed the digger, so how could he have stood trial first?
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא teaches that the ox killed him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אילא's answer. If the ox killed him, there was no time for a trial.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording of the ברייתא suggests the digger died on the spot. A dead man cannot be judged, so the debt could not have been fixed by a court.

keyTerms.meaning: it killed him
it is taught (in the ברייתא)

phrases.english: But it teaches "it killed him"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אילא's claim that the digger stood trial
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says the ox killed him, which leaves no time for a trial

steps.title: The ox made him a טריפה
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה explains that 'killed' means the ox gave him a fatal wound, and he lived long enough to be judged.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said: it means the ox made him a טריפה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the word 'killed' so that a trial still fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A טריפה has a deadly wound but can live for some time. The ברייתא calls him 'killed' because he is sure to die. There was still time for the court to rule before he died.

keyTerms.meaning: someone with a fatal wound who will die within twelve months

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
Where it made him a tereifa.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה כְּשֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ טְרֵיפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Killed him' means he died right away
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Killed him' means a fatal wound, with time left for a trial

steps.title: חגא's version: he died and was buried
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes חגא's version of the ברייתא, which says the digger died and was buried, so a טריפה cannot be meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב נחמן said that חגא teaches: he died and it buried him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the טריפה answer with another version of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In חגא's version, the ox fell on the digger and he died and was buried right there in the pit. That is clearly an immediate death, so the טריפה answer does not fit.

keyTerms.meaning: he died and it buried him

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Naḥman say that Ḥagga teaches:
He died and it buried him!
phrases.notes: The ox fell on him and he was buried right in the pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן תָּנֵי חַגָּא מֵת וּקְבָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 7
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: חגא's version describes an immediate death and burial, which leaves no time for a trial

steps.title: Judges sat at the mouth of the pit
steps.stepSummary: The case is where judges were right at the pit and ruled before he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ruling in the ברייתא is a case where judges sat at the opening of the pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a court was right there and ruled on the debt in his last moments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even with a quick death, a court sitting at the pit could rule before he died. So the debt was fixed by a court, and רבה's view still holds.

keyTerms.meaning: judges
at the mouth of the pit

steps.whatToRemember: According to the view that a debt written in the תורה is not like a שטר (רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, as רבה explains him), heirs pay a damages debt only if a court ruled on it during the person's lifetime.

phrases.english: And the ruling is where judges sat
phrases.notes: Here 'הילכתא' does not mean the final halacha. It means the law of the ברייתא is talking about this case.

phrases.english: at the opening of the pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case to an unusual scenario
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A sudden death leaves no time for a court ruling
steps.terutzMaskana: Judges were present and ruled before he died

steps.title: Offerings of a man going out to be executed
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: we sprinkle the blood of his earlier offerings for him, but we do not wait for an offering he became obligated in at that moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: for a man going out to be executed, we sprinkle the blood of his חטאת and אשם for him. If he sinned at that time, we do not take care of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a condemned man's offerings. This opens a new topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא makes a split. If his offering is already underway, its blood is sprinkled before he dies. But if he only now became obligated in a new offering, the execution does not wait for it.

keyTerms.meaning: one going out to be executed
they sprinkle (the blood on the מזבח)
sin offering
guilt offering
we do not attend to him

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One going out to be executed —
they sprinkle for him from the blood of his sin offering
and from the blood of his guilt offering;
if he sinned at that time —
they do not attend to him.
phrases.notes: The execution is not held up so he can bring the new offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on a related topic: a condemned man's obligations
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Earlier offerings are completed before the execution; new obligations do not delay it

steps.title: Why don't we wait for the new offering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the second ruling of the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the court does not wait for the new offering. It is setting up רב יוסף's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave a ruling without a reason. The גמרא wants to know why a new offering is ignored.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind step 10
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the court does not wait for a new offering

steps.title: We may not drag out his execution
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף explains that delaying the execution would be cruel to the condemned man.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: because we may not torment him by delaying his judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives the reason: waiting would cause the condemned man extra suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making a man wait for his execution is a kind of torment. So the court does not hold things up to bring a new offering.

keyTerms.meaning: we do not torment him by delaying his sentence

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Because we may not afflict him by delaying his judgment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף מִפְּנֵי שֶׁאֵין מְעַנִּין אֶת דִּינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Delaying the execution would torment the condemned man

steps.title: Then why wait in the first case?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks: if delay is forbidden, we should not wait to sprinkle the blood of his earlier offerings either.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: if so, even in the first part of the ברייתא we should not wait!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רב יוסף's reason using the first half of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half says we sprinkle the blood of his earlier offerings, which also takes time. If any delay is torment, that should be forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: if so
the first part (of the ברייתא)

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: If so,
even the first clause as well!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי אִי הָכִי אֲפִילּוּ רֵישָׁא נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יוסף's reason from step 12
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's reason: no delaying the execution
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first half of the ברייתא does allow a delay for his earlier offerings

steps.title: The animal was already slaughtered
steps.stepSummary: The first case is where his offering was already slaughtered, so only a short delay for sprinkling remains.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where his offering was already slaughtered at that time.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers אביי: in the first case the offering was already slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the animal is slaughtered, only the sprinkling is left, which takes very little time. Such a tiny delay is not torment. Bringing a brand new offering would take much longer.

keyTerms.meaning: his offering was already slaughtered

steps.whatToRemember: A condemned man's execution waits only for a nearly finished offering, never for a new one, so his suffering is not dragged out.

phrases.english: Such as where his offering was slaughtered
at that time.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּגוֹן שֶׁהָיָה זִבְחוֹ זָבוּחַ בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the first clause to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause allows a real delay for his offerings
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the sprinkling remains, so the delay is too short to count as torment

steps.title: What if his offering was not yet slaughtered?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if the ruling is only about an offering already slaughtered, the ברייתא should have taught the not-yet-slaughtered case as its contrast instead of a new case of sinning at that moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we wait only when the offering is already slaughtered, then what about an offering not yet slaughtered? We don't wait? Then instead of teaching 'if he sinned at that time we don't attend to him,' the ברייתא should have drawn the line within the same case: this applies when it was slaughtered, but if not slaughtered, we don't wait.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes on the answer from Step 14. If the ברייתא only waits for an offering that was already slaughtered, it should have said so directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 said we wait only because the offering was already slaughtered. That means an unslaughtered offering would not be waited for. If so, the ברייתא could have made its point with that contrast, so why did it switch to a different case, a man who sinned at that moment?

keyTerms.meaning: an offering that has already been slaughtered
let it make the distinction within that same case
we attend to his needs (here, his offering)
in what case was this said? (a limiting formula)

phrases.english: But if his offering was not yet slaughtered, what is the law?
We do not wait?
Instead of teaching "he sinned at that time,
we do not attend to him,"
let it distinguish and teach within that very case:
In what case are these words said?
When the offering was already slaughtered at that time;
but if the offering was not slaughtered, no!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּתָנֵי חָטָא בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה אֵין נִזְקָקִין לוֹ לִיפְלוֹג וְלִיתְנֵי בְּדִידַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא in light of Step 14's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: The way the ברייתא is worded, given the answer of Step 14
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the key line is slaughtered versus not slaughtered, the ברייתא should have taught that contrast in the same case instead of a new case of sinning at that moment.

steps.title: An unslaughtered offering counts like sinning at that moment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא does mean this: an offering not yet slaughtered is treated like an obligation that arose just now, so we do not wait.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is exactly what it means: this applies when the offering was already slaughtered. But if it was not slaughtered, he is treated like someone who sinned at that moment, and we do not attend to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is saying exactly what Step 15 suggested. The case of 'sinned at that time' includes an offering that was not yet slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא was not ignoring the unslaughtered case. It put that case into the same group as a fresh sin, because in both a long delay would be needed. So the line falls between 'already slaughtered' (only a short wait) and everything else (no waiting).

keyTerms.meaning: that is indeed what it is saying
he is treated like one who sinned

steps.whatToRemember: We wait only to sprinkle the blood of an offering already slaughtered. If it was not yet slaughtered, it is like a new obligation, and the execution is not delayed.

phrases.english: That is indeed what it is saying:
In what case are these words said?
When the offering was already slaughtered at that time;
but if the offering was not slaughtered,
he is treated like one who sinned at that time,
and we do not attend to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 15 by reading the ברייתא's 'sinned at that time' to include an unslaughtered offering
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the case already given in the ברייתא includes the case asked about
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא skipped the not-yet-slaughtered case and should have mentioned it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The not-yet-slaughtered case is treated as 'sinned at that time,' so it is covered by the ruling that we do not wait.

steps.title: משנה: a pregnant woman going to execution, and benefiting from the executed
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a pregnant woman going to execution is not delayed until she gives birth, unless she is already in labor. One may benefit from an executed woman's hair, but not from an executed animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman who goes out to be executed: we do not wait for her until she gives birth. A woman already sitting on the birthing stool: we wait for her until she gives birth. A woman who was executed: one may benefit from her hair. An animal that was executed: it is forbidden to benefit from it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with four short rulings. Two are about delaying an execution for a birth, and two are about benefiting from someone or something that was executed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before labor, the fetus is treated as part of the mother, so the execution goes ahead. Once she is in labor, the baby is treated as a separate person, so we wait. An executed animal is forbidden to benefit from, but the משנה allows benefit from an executed woman's hair.

keyTerms.meaning: our משנה
we wait / delay
the birthing stool, meaning she is already in labor
forbidden to derive any benefit from

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the first two cases. Before labor we do NOT wait. Once she is on the birthing stool, in labor, we DO wait.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
A woman who went out to be executed,
we do not wait for her until she gives birth.
A woman who sat on the birthing stool,
we wait for her until she gives birth.
A woman who was executed: one may benefit from her hair.
An animal that was executed is forbidden for benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה opens a new topic, while staying with the theme of delaying an execution
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not delay execution for a pregnancy, but do delay once labor has begun. An executed woman's hair is permitted for benefit; an executed animal is forbidden for benefit.

steps.title: Isn't it obvious? The fetus is part of her body
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needs to say we do not wait for a pregnant woman to give birth, since the fetus is just part of her body.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious! The fetus is her own body!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first ruling of the משנה as unnecessary. Since the fetus is part of the mother, of course her execution includes it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before birth, the fetus is treated as part of the mother, like a limb. So there seems to be no reason to think we would delay, and the ruling looks too obvious to teach.

keyTerms.meaning: it is obvious (a challenge that a ruling is not needed)
it is her own body

phrases.english: GEMARA:
It is obvious; it is her own body!
phrases.notes: "It" is the fetus. Before birth it counts as part of the mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the משנה's first ruling needs to be taught
steps.kashyaTarget: The first ruling of the משנה, that we do not wait until she gives birth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The fetus is part of the mother's body, so the ruling seems too obvious to need teaching.

steps.title: We might have thought the fetus is the husband's property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ruling was needed: a פסוק calls the fetus's value the husband's money, so we might have delayed the execution to protect his property. The משנה teaches that we do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed. You might have said: since it is written 'as the woman's husband shall place upon him,' the fetus is the husband's money, and we should not make him lose it. So the משנה teaches us that we do not wait.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה's ruling is not obvious. There was a real reason to think the court should wait.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about men who strike a pregnant woman gives the payment for the fetus to the husband. This suggests the fetus is his property, a separate interest from the mother. The משנה teaches that this does not delay the execution.

keyTerms.meaning: it was necessary to teach
you might have thought to say
the husband's money / property
it teaches us

steps.whatToRemember: Even though the fetus has money value for the husband, a pregnant woman's execution is not delayed for it.

phrases.english: It was necessary; it might enter your mind to say:

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וּכְתִיב ״כַּאֲשֶׁר יָשִׁית עָלָיו בַּעַל הָאִשָּׁה״,
phrases.english: Since it is written: "as the woman's husband shall place upon him,"
the fetus is the husband's money,
and we should not make him lose it,
so the משנה teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 18 by showing a real reason someone might have thought the court should wait
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a reasonable mistaken thought (סלקא דעתך) that the משנה comes to reject
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because of the פסוק, the fetus is the husband's property, so the court should wait until birth to avoid causing him a loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court does not wait. The husband's money interest does not delay the execution.

steps.title: Why not really delay for the husband's sake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: if the fetus is the husband's money, maybe we really should wait until she gives birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that indeed we should wait!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the end of the last step. If the fetus is the husband's property, maybe we really should delay the execution.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 19, the husband's ownership of the fetus was only a הוה אמינא that the משנה rejects. Now the גמרא asks why that thought is wrong. Maybe the husband's money really should be protected by waiting for the birth.

keyTerms.meaning: But say (introduces a suggestion that challenges what was just said)
Indeed so; that really is the law

phrases.english: But say that indeed [we wait]!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the הוה אמינא from Step 19 and asks why it should not be the actual law.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that we do not wait for a pregnant woman to give birth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since a פסוק treats the fetus's value as the husband's money, protecting it by waiting seems reasonable.

steps.title: A פסוק includes the fetus in the death
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו in the name of רבי יוחנן brings the פסוק 'ומתו גם שניהם', which comes to include the fetus.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The פסוק says 'they shall also both of them die' to include the fetus.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק showing that the Torah itself includes the fetus in the mother's death. So we do not wait.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra words in the פסוק about adulterers dying are read as adding the fetus. Since the Torah itself wants the fetus included, the husband's money claim does not delay the execution.

keyTerms.meaning: To include; to add something not stated outright
Fetus; child

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the משנה's ruling a source in a פסוק. The Torah itself includes the fetus in the mother's death, so the husband's claim to it does not delay the execution.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
The verse says: "They shall also both of them die"
to include the fetus.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 20 with a Torah source.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might wait to protect the husband's money in the fetus.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah includes the fetus in the death, so we do not wait.

steps.title: That פסוק is already used by רבי יאשיה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that רבי יאשיה needs this same phrase to teach that both sinners must be equal.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this phrase is needed to teach that they are not punished unless both of them are equal. These are the words of רבי יאשיה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's source. The same words are already being used for a different rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה learns from 'both of them' that the man and woman are only punished if they are equal, both adults. If the phrase is used up for that rule, it cannot also teach about the fetus.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it for (this source is already used for another teaching)
Equal (here: both are adults)

phrases.english: But this is needed for him
[to teach that they are not punished] until both of them are equal,
phrases.notes: Equal means both are adults. If one is a minor, the adult is not punished with death for this sin.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source just brought in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's use of 'ומתו גם שניהם' to include the fetus
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One phrase normally cannot teach two different rules. רבי יאשיה already uses it for the equality rule.

steps.title: The fetus comes from the word 'also'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the fetus is learned from the extra word 'גם', not from 'שניהם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we said it, we meant from the word 'also'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by splitting the פסוק. The fetus is learned from the word 'גם', and רבי יאשיה's rule comes from 'שניהם'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each teaching comes from a different word, so there is no overlap. 'שניהם' teaches that both must be equal, and the extra word 'גם' adds the fetus.

keyTerms.meaning: When we said it (we meant...): clarifies what was meant
Also: an extra word read as adding something

steps.whatToRemember: The fetus dies with its mother because of the word 'גם'. This is why we do not delay the execution of a pregnant woman.

phrases.english: When we said it, [we learned it] from "also."
phrases.notes: So 'both of them' stays free for רבי יאשיה, and the extra word 'also' adds the fetus.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי יוחנן's source against the challenge in Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the פסוק: different words teach different rules
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole phrase 'גם שניהם' is used up by רבי יאשיה.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'שניהם' teaches equality, and 'גם' includes the fetus.

steps.title: Why wait once she is in labor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's exception of a woman sitting on the birthing stool and asks for its reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'She sat on the birthing stool, etc.' What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's exception. If she is already in labor, we wait, and the גמרא asks why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just learned that the fetus dies with the mother. So why should labor change anything? The גמרא wants to know what is different once labor has started.

keyTerms.meaning: Birthing stool; being in active labor
Etc.: the rest of the quoted line
What is the reason?

phrases.english: [The משנה said:] She sat on the birthing stool, etc.
What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָשְׁבָה עַל הַמַּשְׁבֵּר וְכוּ׳. מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the main rule to the משנה's exception.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why labor makes us delay, when the fetus normally dies with the mother

steps.title: Once the baby moves, it is a separate body
steps.stepSummary: Once the fetus has moved from its place, it counts as a separate body and cannot be killed with her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since it has moved from its place, it is a different body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that once the baby starts coming out, it is no longer part of the mother. So we must not kill it with her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק only includes a fetus that is still part of her body. Once labor uproots the baby, it is its own person. That is why the court waits for the birth.

keyTerms.meaning: Uprooted: the fetus has moved from its place to come out
A different body; a separate person

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the line where the fetus stops being part of the mother: the start of labor.

phrases.english: Since it has moved from its place,
it is a different body.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Once the fetus has moved to come out, it is a separate person and cannot be included in her execution.

steps.title: שמואל: strike the womb so the fetus dies first
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that a pregnant woman going to execution is struck on the womb first, so the fetus dies first and she is not disgraced.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: A woman going out to be executed is struck against her womb, so that the fetus dies first, so that she does not come to disgrace.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a new practical rule. Before the execution, the court strikes the pregnant woman's womb so that the fetus dies first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that after she dies, the live fetus might come out and she would be publicly disgraced. Killing the fetus first prevents this.

keyTerms.meaning: The woman going out to be executed
The womb
Disgrace; shameful exposure

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
A [pregnant] woman going out to be executed,
they strike her against the womb,
so that the fetus dies first,
so that she does not come to disgrace.
phrases.notes: The disgrace is the baby coming out and bleeding after her death, in front of everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הָאִשָּׁה הַיּוֹצְאָה לֵיהָרֵג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new ruling about how the execution of a pregnant woman is carried out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Strike the womb before the execution so the fetus dies first and she is not disgraced.

steps.title: But the fetus naturally dies first anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: his rule assumes the mother dies first, but we hold the fetus dies first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this to say that she would die first? But we hold that the fetus dies first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's ruling. It seems to assume the mother would die before the fetus, which goes against what we know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's worry only makes sense if the fetus could outlive the mother and then come out. But we hold that a fetus always dies before its mother. If so, striking the womb seems pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say? (draws out what a statement implies)
We hold; it is established for us
First

phrases.english: Is this to say that she dies before [the fetus], first?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא קַיְימָא לַן דְּוָולָד מָיֵית בְּרֵישָׁא!
phrases.english: But we hold that the fetus dies first!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּהִיא קָדְמָה וּמֵתָה בְּרֵישָׁא? וְהָא קַיְימָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind שמואל's ruling in Step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling to strike the womb so the fetus dies first
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל's rule assumes the mother dies first, but the accepted fact is that the fetus dies first, so the rule seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The source for the idea that a fetus dies first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה that a one-day-old baby inherits and passes on inheritance. רב ששת explains that this refers to inheriting his mother's property and passing it to his brothers from his father.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: a one-day-old baby inherits and bequeaths. רב ששת explained: he inherits his mother's property, and if he then dies, it passes to his brothers from his father.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing the source behind the challenge to שמואל from the last step. This sets up the next step, which shows how this source proves the fetus dies first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, a mother's property goes to her own family. But if her baby lived even a moment after her, he inherits it first. When he dies, it goes to his heirs, including half-brothers from his father who are not her relatives.

keyTerms.meaning: A baby one day old
Inherits and passes on an inheritance
The mother's property
Brothers from the father, meaning half-brothers with a different mother

phrases.english: As we learned: a baby one day old
inherits and bequeaths.
And רב ששת says:
He inherits his mother's property
to bequeath it to his brothers from the father.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: תִּינוֹק בֶּן יוֹמוֹ נוֹחֵל וּמַנְחִיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the claim in step 27 that the fetus dies first.
steps.raayaObject: The assumption that a fetus dies before its mother
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in נדה about a one-day-old baby, explained by רב ששת

steps.title: How the source shows the fetus dies first
steps.stepSummary: Only a born baby inherits from his mother this way, not a fetus. A fetus is presumed to die first, and a son cannot inherit from his mother after he is already in the grave.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is only true of a one-day-old baby, but not a fetus. A fetus dies first, and a son does not inherit his mother from the grave to pass her property to his brothers from his father.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the point of the source: a fetus is treated as dying before its mother. So שמואל, who assumes the mother dies first, seems to be wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה stresses a baby who was already born. This implies a fetus does not inherit, because it died before its mother and was never alive to inherit her. That clashes with שמואל's worry that the mother would die first and then be disgraced by the fetus.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifically, only in this case
A fetus, an unborn baby
Dies first

keyTerms.term: אֵין הַבֵּן יוֹרֵשׁ אֶת אִמּוֹ בְּקֶבֶר
keyTerms.meaning: A son does not inherit his mother while he is in the grave

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about inheritance laws for their own sake. The inheritance rule is only being used to prove the order of death, which is what matters for שמואל.

phrases.english: Specifically a baby one day old,
but a fetus, no,
because it dies first,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין הַבֵּן יוֹרֵשׁ אֶת אִמּוֹ בְּקֶבֶר
phrases.english: and a son does not inherit his mother in the grave
to bequeath to his brothers from the father!

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּוְוקָא בֶּן יוֹם אֶחָד, אֲבָל עוּבָּר — לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from the source quoted in step 28.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה implies a fetus dies before its mother, but שמואל assumes the mother dies first.

steps.title: The fetus dies first only in a natural death
steps.stepSummary: The rule that the fetus dies first applies only to natural death, when the weak fetus is quickly killed. When the mother is killed, she dies first.
steps.simpleTranslation: That applies to natural death. Since the fetus's life is weak, the drop of מלאך המות enters and cuts its סימנים. But if she was killed, she dies first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל by limiting the rule. A fetus dies first only when the mother dies naturally, not when she is executed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a natural death, the fetus's weak life ends right away. In an execution, the killing blow hits the mother directly, so she dies before the fetus. שמואל was speaking about execution, so his concern that the fetus might come out after her death makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: This applies only to the following case
Its life force is small and weak
The drop of the Angel of Death
The windpipe and food pipe, the organs cut in שחיטה
She was killed, for example executed

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the order of death depends on how the mother dies. That distinction keeps both the inheritance rule and שמואל's ruling standing.

phrases.english: This applies to a natural death,
since the fetus's life force is small,
the drop of the Angel of Death enters
and cuts its סימנים,
phrases.notes: The fetus is killed from the inside right away, so it goes before its mother.

phrases.english: but if she was killed, she dies first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 27–29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between cases: natural death versus being killed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A fetus always dies before its mother, which would make שמואל's concern pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fetus dies first only in a natural death. In an execution the mother dies first, as שמואל assumes.

steps.title: A story where the fetus moved after its mother died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that the fetus dies first in a natural death. There was a case where the fetus moved three times after its mother died.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there was an incident, and the fetus jerked up to three times!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea that in a natural death the fetus always dies first. It brings a real case where the fetus seemed alive after the mother died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the fetus moved after its mother's natural death, it seems it was still alive and did not die first. That would undo the distinction made in the last step.

keyTerms.meaning: An actual incident that happened
Jerked, twitched
Twitches, jerking movements

phrases.english: But there was an incident,
and it jerked up to three times!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in step 30 that the fetus dies first in a natural death.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that in a natural death the fetus dies first
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A fetus that moved after its mother's natural death seems to have still been alive.

steps.title: The movement is like a lizard's twitching tail
steps.stepSummary: The movement was not a sign of life. It was like the tail of a lizard that keeps twitching after it is cut off.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is just like the tail of a lizard, which twitches.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the fetus's movements were only twitching, not real life. So the fetus did die first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cut-off lizard tail moves even though it is not alive. In the same way, the fetus's three jerks were leftover motion after death, so the rule from step 30 still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It is just like
The tail of a lizard

steps.whatToRemember: In a natural death the fetus dies before its mother, and any movement afterward is only twitching. When the mother is executed, she dies first, which is why שמואל has the womb struck first.

phrases.english: It is just like the tail of a lizard
which twitches.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the evidence: the movement was not a sign of life
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fetus's movements show it outlived its mother.
steps.terutzMaskana: The movements were lifeless twitching, so the fetus did die first.

steps.title: On שבת we cut open a mother who died in labor to save the baby
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes שמואל: if a woman in labor dies on שבת, we bring a knife, cut open her belly, and take out the baby.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: If a woman sat on the birthing chair and died on שבת, we bring a knife, cut open her belly, and take out the baby.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling: if a woman dies while giving birth on שבת, we cut her open to get the baby out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling assumes the baby might still be alive after the mother died, so we act to save it even on שבת. This connects to the earlier steps about whether the baby or the mother dies first. Here the concern is clear: the baby may still be alive.

keyTerms.meaning: The birthing chair a woman sat on during labor
Her belly
The baby (still inside the mother)
The Sabbath, when cutting and carrying are normally limited

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that saving a baby who may still be alive is important enough to act on שבת, even when the mother has already died.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Shmuel said:
A woman who sat on the birthing chair
and died on Shabbat,
we bring a knife,
and cut open her belly,
and take out the baby.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new ruling related to the earlier discussion of whether a baby can live after its mother dies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a woman dies in labor on שבת, we cut her open with a knife and take out the baby.

steps.title: Why does this ruling even need to be said?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: this is obvious. What forbidden act is the person doing by cutting her?
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious! What is he doing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's ruling as too obvious to need saying. This question sets up the next move, where the גמרא will explain what the ruling adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of the question is that cutting a dead body does not seem to be a real forbidden act on שבת. If no forbidden act is happening, why would we need a special ruling to allow it? Now the גמרא has to find something in the ruling that is not obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious; why say it?
What is he doing? (meaning: what forbidden act is he doing?)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying cutting her open is wrong. It is saying the ruling is so clearly allowed that it should not need to be said.

phrases.english: It is obvious!
What is he doing?
phrases.notes: He means: what forbidden act is the person cutting her doing? It doesn't seem like any.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's ruling as stating something too obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for שמואל's ruling in step 33
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Cutting a dead body does not seem to be any forbidden act on שבת, so a ruling allowing it seems unnecessary.
